terms.meaning: A standard text address format, here used to tell SQLite how to open a file.
A way of opening a database so that the program can read it but cannot change it.
Replacing characters that have special meaning in an address with a safe code.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Imports and purpose
sections.what: Loads the path and URL-encoding tools and states that the file keeps normal paths separate from database address text.
sections.why: Likely reason: mixing the two is a common source of bugs, so the file has one job.

sections.name: readonly_uri
sections.title: Building the read-only address
sections.what: Turns a file path into a read-only database address by encoding it and adding the read-only setting, with comments on Windows long-path handling.
sections.why: Likely reason: the address must be exact, or SQLite may open a different file or refuse to open the database.
sections.watch_out: The list of characters left unencoded controls Windows path handling, so changing it needs testing on Windows.

summary: Converts a normal file path into the special address form that the SQLite library uses to open a database read-only.
purpose: Lets the app open project databases safely in read-only mode, even when the file path contains characters with special meaning.
why: Likely reason: a path with a question mark or hash sign would otherwise be read as part of the address and open the wrong file or fail.
how: Takes the path, encodes every character except colons and slashes, and adds the read-only setting at the end.
inputs: A file path to a database.
outputs: A text address that the SQLite library accepts for a read-only connection.
risks: If the safe characters are changed, Windows long paths or special characters can break. If the read-only setting is removed, the app could write to the database.
debug: If opening a database fails for a path with special characters, print the generated address and check the escaping. Check the platform, since Windows paths behave differently.
